title: A Stolen Vineyard and a Murder
overview: King Ahab wants a neighbor's vineyard, Queen Jezebel has the owner falsely accused and killed, and the prophet Elijah confronts the king with God's judgment.

parts.label: Ahab wants Naboth's vineyard (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: In Israel, family land was seen as a gift from God that was meant to stay in the family for good, so Naboth's refusal came from faith and loyalty to his ancestors. Ahab offers a fair deal but cannot accept a no, and he goes to bed sulking and refusing food.

parts.label: Jezebel's plot (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: Jezebel mocks Ahab for not acting like a king, then sends orders stamped with his seal ring, which gave them royal authority. A public fast hinted that the town carried some serious guilt, and the law required two witnesses for a death sentence, so she arranges two liars.

parts.label: Naboth is stoned (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: The town leaders carry out the scheme, and Naboth is stoned outside the city on the false charge of cursing God and the king. A later passage says his sons were killed too, which may be how the land passed to the king, though exactly how is not certain.

parts.label: Elijah confronts Ahab (vv. 17-24)
parts.note: Elijah meets Ahab in the very vineyard he took and names the crime plainly: murder, then seizing the land. Dogs will lick Ahab's blood as they did Naboth's, dogs will eat Jezebel at Jezreel, and Ahab's family line will end like two earlier royal families, its dead left unburied, which was a deep disgrace then.

parts.label: The writer's verdict (vv. 25-26)
parts.note: The writer steps in to say no king gave himself over to evil like Ahab, urged on by Jezebel. He compares Ahab's idol worship to that of the Amorites, peoples who lived in the land before Israel.

parts.label: Ahab humbles himself (vv. 27-29)
parts.note: Ahab tears his clothes and wears sackcloth, a rough cloth worn in grief, and God delays the disaster until his son's time. Later chapters tell of dogs licking Ahab's blood, his son's body thrown onto Naboth's land, and Jezebel's death, and many readers find it troubling that the punishment falls on the next generation.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Ahab's humbling was a real change of heart or a passing fear, since he carries on as before in the next chapter, and so on what God's response here shows about partial repentance.
think: When someone powerful wants something, what makes ordinary people go along with an injustice they know is wrong?
